title: The crowd that never buys, and the lights that come back

turns.t: Good morning, Singapore — it's Saturday, the fifth of September. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let's go.
Three headlines before the coffee's cold. One — the Gulf war finally cracks open a door.
[curious] A door? After a month of nothing but which base got hit?
A door. We'll get there. Two — the American jobs number lands like a slammed one, and the rate-hike debate is back.
[wry] And three, my favourite, the grown-ups who never put the LEGO away.
[deadpan] I knew you'd claim that one.
[laughs] I've earned it. Start with the war, though — the serious thing first.

Right. Overnight into the first of September, the United States hit about a hundred Revolutionary Guard targets around the Strait of Hormuz — and this time the mine-laying ships too. The heaviest single exchange in over a month.
[exhales] And Iran answered?
On the same pattern it's kept all summer. Missiles and drones at American bases in Jordan, Kuwait and Bahrain. No American casualties reported.
So they're still hitting property and pride, not people.

Mostly. There's a disputed one at sea — a tanker called the Sidr, and an Iranian claim that two tankers struck mines. Central Command flatly denies it. Both can't be true, so we're holding that number, not printing it.
[thoughtful] Okay. And the door?
At a summit in Bishkek, Iran's president said Iran would return — his word — immediately to the June ceasefire the moment Washington restores its own commitments.
[pause] That's the first concrete thing either side has said in weeks.

It's an offer, not a deal — and Washington hasn't answered it yet. But after a month where the only news was which base got hit, and which tanker, an offer to reciprocate is the story that's actually new. Whether it's taken is next week's.
And the oil? Because a fifth of the world's seaborne crude moves through that strait.
Brent's above ninety-five dollars. But here's the tell — the market is pricing the risk of a closure, not a closure. Ships are still moving, just fewer and dearer.
[curious] Which means a real ceasefire could reopen the flow faster than the headlines suggest.
That's the contrarian read, and it's a good one. Some of the closure is insurers and owners just avoiding a war-risk premium. Watch the tanker count, not the press releases.
Speaking of numbers that moved everything — the jobs report.
Friday. American payrolls rose a hundred and sixty-two thousand in August. Consensus was about fifty-five. So roughly three times what the room expected.
[gasps] Three times? That's a slammed door, all right.
Unemployment steady at four point one per cent. And the one dovish thread — wages actually cooled, to three point one per cent on the year.
So walk me through what that does. Hot jobs, cooler pay — where does it land?
[thoughtful] Strong data is bad data right now. Rate-hike odds for September jumped toward the high fifties per cent. Yields up, the dollar firmer, stocks slipped.
And the two things people watch for fear — gold and bitcoin?

Both gave ground. Gold had run toward forty-five hundred dollars an ounce on some dovish Fed remarks earlier in the week, then handed about two per cent back. It's near its high, though — not a fifth below it, whatever you may have heard.
And bitcoin?

Back below eighty thousand. It's the high-beta liquidity read, so on a hawkish day it's the first to flinch — and its volatility is worth naming on a day the move was sharp. This is analysis, by the way, not advice.
[wry] The lawyers thank you. So is the hike locked in?
No. One strong month, cooler wages, joblessness still at four-one — that doesn't clinch it. And these payroll prints get revised hard. The tell to wait for is the next inflation number.
Home, then. Singapore had a rough headline this week.
Fifty-two Singaporeans arrested and detained in Guangxi, in southern China, over a suspected pyramid scheme. It's believed to be the largest single overseas detention of citizens on record.
[sighs] Fifty-two. How does that happen in twenty twenty-six?
Because it doesn't arrive from a stranger. Guangxi is the home of the old nineteen-forty Sunshine scheme and all its rebrands. The pitch travels through a cousin, a former colleague, a church friend.
So the red flag isn't the promised return.

It's the ask — recruit others, pay a large sum up front. That's the tell, whoever's smiling when they say it. And one honest caveat: in these schemes the line between victim and recruiter blurs. Fifty-two detained isn't fifty-two innocents.
And the air — I had to shut the windows Thursday night.

The haze is back. The twenty-four-hour reading crossed a hundred into the unhealthy band for the first time since twenty twenty-three, fires in Sumatra and Kalimantan. Dust off the purifier this weekend.
[wry] Though it's a long way from the twenty-fifteen crisis.

An order of magnitude below it — the twenty-fifteen crisis topped three hundred. A monsoon shift can clear this one in a day or two. But the purifier and the N-ninety-fives come out, and the outdoor run waits for the weekend.
All right. Let's spend a little. The Atelier this week is wristwatch straps — and this one's practically written for you.
[amused] For the man with more straps than watches, yes. The lesson is that in this climate, the honest answer often isn't leather at all.
Wait — really? The whole culture is leather.
And leather on a tropical wrist is half-consumable — six to twelve months before sweat darkens and rots it. The buy-once material here is F-K-M rubber. Shrugs off sweat, barely degrades.
But if you want leather?

Shell cordovan — the dense membrane from a horse's rump, it ripples instead of cracking. And the lovely local fact: the reader's home team, Delugs, is Singapore-based. Shell straps around two hundred and fifteen dollars, alligator around two sixty-five.
And the sceptic? There's always a sceptic.

[deadpan] The clasp does the paying. A genuine Rolex rubber strap runs seven hundred and sixty-five dollars to nearly a thousand. A functionally identical aftermarket one is a hundred and fifty. You're buying the signed buckle, not the band.
[laughs] The clasp does the paying. I'm stealing that.
Onto the machines. Nvidia wrote MediaTek a cheque this week — three and a half billion dollars.
To buy them?

To lend them, technically — convertible bonds. But the real purchase is a standard. MediaTek's custom chips will now plug into Nvidia's rack over its own interconnect. The analysts called it a tollbooth for custom silicon.
[skeptical] So everyone else's chip pays Nvidia a toll to sit near an Nvidia chip.

That's the shape of it. And the sceptics call it circular financing — Nvidia's return is tied to growth inside Nvidia's own ecosystem. It's a real moat or an accounting entry, depending on whether a named customer ever ships one.
For the home-lab crowd, anything runnable this week?

The pick is a dense model called Qwen three-point-eight twenty-seven-B. Fits a twenty-four-gigabyte card at short context — but push it to a long context and it spills, and you're buying a thirty-two-gigabyte card anyway.
[thoughtful] So thirty-two gigs is where it stops being a compromise.
Exactly the line the testers landed on. Local for privacy, the cloud for the genuinely hard problems.
And a gadget I can actually hold?
Sennheiser's flagship earbuds, the Momentum True Wireless Five. Two hundred and ninety-nine dollars and ninety-five cents — same price as the last generation.
That's not the news, though, is it. You've got that look.
[warmly] The news is a battery you can replace. In the buds and the case both. Every sealed rival is a two-year consumable the day you buy it.
[excited] Finally. That's the buy-once thing done right.
With one honest catch — the noise cancelling, much improved, still sits below the Sony and Bose and Apple elite. Buy it for the sound and the longevity, not for silence on a plane.
And the object of the week — the one I actually want.
[amused] I know exactly which one. MB&F and a French clockmaker made a mechanical table clock inspired by the film Alien. It's called the Nostromo, after the ship.
[curious] Go on.
It ships as two hundred and twenty-two loose parts, in a box, with tools. You build it yourself — over about ten hours.
[laughs] Ten hours! That's a whole weekend. I love it. How much?
Twelve thousand Swiss francs. About fourteen thousand eight hundred US dollars, fifty pieces only.
[sighs] Oh.
And the sceptic notes it runs on an existing movement — a base version is about five and a half thousand euros. So the premium buys the design, not new mechanics.
[wry] It's a five-figure LEGO set for grown men.
[deadpan] Which is a perfect handoff, and you know it.
[excited] Right — take my hand. We're going down the rabbit hole.
[sighs] Every week with this.
[laughs] Every week. LEGO for adults. There's a word — A-F-O-L. Adult Fan Of LEGO.
And it is not buying your kid a set. It's grown adults buying, building and displaying it for themselves. LEGO built a whole matte-black eighteen-plus line for them.
How big is this, really?

Big enough that adults now drive an estimated fifth to a quarter of a company worth about thirteen billion US dollars a year. Its biggest single set is a Death Star — nine thousand and twenty-three pieces, a thousand dollars.
[gasps] A thousand dollars for one set?

And here's the twist — the community wasn't kind. One review called it spectacular in scale but hollow at heart. It's a thirty-inch disc, not the enclosed sphere people pictured. Cavernous gaps, for a thousand dollars.
[laughs] Brutal. So is LEGO a good investment or not? I keep hearing it beats stocks.

[skeptical] That's the myth, and there's a real study behind it — a couple of Russian economists, twenty-three hundred sets, about eleven per cent a year. But it's survivorship-heavy. It measures the sets that went up.
Ah. Most sets don't.
Most never beat inflation. Only the retired, limited ones pop. The honest line from the community itself — buy to build and display, treat any gain as a bonus, not a thesis.
[warmly] That's genuinely good advice for the whole hobby, isn't it. Build the thing.

Build the thing. And if you're starting — lurk first on the forums, then a botanical set for eighty-odd dollars to test the tactile pull, then a modular building for the real question of whether you're an A-F-O-L. About eight hundred and forty-five Singapore dollars, all in, and you're properly down the hole.
[laughs] You've costed out my midlife crisis. Thank you.
A few quick ones from culture and the body, before the close.
The film festival — did Venice give out its big prize?
Not yet. The Golden Lion lands on the twelfth. So if a search engine tells you the twenty-twenty-six winner, it's lying — that's last year's, bleeding in.
And music?

A country song did something historic. Ella Langley's Choosin' Texas hit its twentieth week at number one — the longest-running non-holiday number one in the chart's history. Only a Mariah Carey Christmas song sits ahead.
[amused] Of course it does. Family desk — anything for the twelve-year-old?
A useful finding. A new study says it's the age they start social media that predicts anxiety more than whether they have an account at all.
[thoughtful] So delay the account, not the phone.
That's the read. And watch for dependence — can she put it down when called to dinner — not the minutes on a dashboard. General guidance, not medical advice.
And for us mid-forties types?

[wry] Strength banks over decades and shows up at the end. A big study tied grip strength to survival — but it's a marker, not a lever. Squeezing a hand-gripper won't buy you the years. Lift something heavy twice a week instead.
And the weekend escape — this one I want.
Iceland. September is the sweet spot — the dark comes back, the roads are still open, and the aurora returns.
[excited] The northern lights. Worth planning a trip around?
Worth planning, but don't pin it on one night. The aurora is a lottery — darkness, clear sky, and geomagnetic luck, all at once. Build four or five clear-night chances.
Anything to know before you go?

[thoughtful] One safety line that matters. The black-sand beach, Reynisfjara — sneaker waves there have killed at least six people since twenty-thirteen, a child last year. Never turn your back to the sea, keep the kids well up the beach.
[thoughtful] Noted. And the famous Blue Lagoon?
The forums have moved on — over-hyped and over-priced. They lean to the Sky Lagoon, or the cheap local pools. Just know a volcano's been erupting nearby on and off, so book it cancellable.
[thoughtful] Chase the light. That's the whole weekend, really.
[warmly] It is. Which brings us, quietly, to the long read.
[warmly] Take your time with this one. It's lovely.
There's a city in South Korea called Daejeon. For years it was the national punchline — the no-fun city. A tidy science town with, people said, nothing to do.
Except?
Except a bakery. Sungsimdang. Founded in nineteen fifty-six by a refugee from the North, in front of the train station. Four shops. All in Daejeon. It refuses to open a single branch anywhere else.
[curious] Four shops. That's it?

Four shops. And last year it earned two hundred and sixty-three billion won — about a hundred and ninety million US dollars. Its operating profit now beats Korea's two national bakery chains combined.
[gasps] Combined? The chains have thousands of stores.

Thousands of outlets, across dozens of countries. And this four-shop house out-earns both of them combined on an advertising budget of one-eighth of one per cent of sales. It gives its unsold bread away at the end of each day, and it baked the loaves for Pope Francis when he visited in twenty-fourteen.
[laughs] How is that possible?

Because you cannot get it anywhere else. The Koreans have a word for the trip — a bread pilgrimage. There's even a single licensed taxi in the city whose driver hands you a menu listing each bakery's predicted sell-out time.
[excited] A bread taxi. That's the most wonderful thing I've heard all week.

[warmly] And here's what it actually means. Korea has a policy word for the slow death of its provinces — regional extinction, as people drain toward Seoul. The usual cures are expensive — a stadium, a factory, a subsidy.
And Daejeon found a cheaper one.
A single, un-scalable institution, seventy years deep. You cannot open it in Seoul, so the only way to have it is to go there. Scarcity, in a country that exports everything, became the product.
[thoughtful] And the copies won't work, will they. You can schedule a festival.

But you have to survive an institution into being. That's the whole argument. The cities that outlast their own shrinking won't be the ones that spent the most — they'll be the ones that had something a chain could never copy, and were wise enough not to dilute it.
[warmly] A no-fun city that learned to rise. On bread.
[warmly] On bread. Which is a better metaphor than we deserve on a Saturday.
[chuckles] It really is.
That's the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-eight pages, footnotes and all.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
